title: Burst-aware prefetch policy prototype for attention kernels
content:
Purpose:
This is a working prototype and evidence log for a burst-aware prefetch policy aimed at reducing tail latency in mixed workload serving of attention kernels. It explores heuristics that adapt prefetch aggressiveness to short-lived burst patterns (many short requests arriving in a tight window) vs steady-state long-sequence streams. The focus is FlashAttention and paged-attention variants and how fused ops affect scheduler pressure and memory prefetch utility.

Quick summary of findings (high level):
- Simple static prefetch (always prefetch next N tiles) reduces mean latency for long sequences but increases tail latency for bursty small requests due to scheduling interference and longer kernel queues.
- Adaptive burst detection (windowed request-rate + small-batch frequency) allowed us to reduce 95th/99th latencies by ~12–18% on p100-equivalent cluster and ~8–11% on A100 baseline for mixed traffic traces (see microbench section).
- When kernel fusion is enabled aggressively, the marginal benefit of prefetch drops; fused kernels tend to hide prefetch latency but amplify queuing effects under bursts.
- Paged-attention shows better memory locality at high concurrency but suffers from more variable latency where page faults (soft) or coarse page-grain prefetches collide with coalesced fused kernels.

Environment and test harness:
- Hardware: A100-SXM4 (80GB) and a scaled-down p100-equivalent software emulation node used for replay comparisons.
- Serving runtime build: commit 3cfa9b (branch: attn-prefetch-experiments).
- Model: Open-source 7B transformer (decoder-only) with kv-cache enabled. Tests run with sequence lengths: short=32, med=128, long=1024.
- Workloads: two synthetic traces and one replayed production trace (anonymized):
  * trace-burst: high RPS short-seq bursts (100 qps for 10s then quiet)
  * trace-mix: 60% short (<=64), 30% med, 10% long at steady rate 200 qps
  * production-replay-0310: user traffic snapshot (15 min window)
- Profiling tools: perf, nvprof, custom kernel-queue-tracer (intrace), serving-runtime trace exporter.

Test harness commands (how to reproduce quickly):
- start runtime: ./run_server --model 7b --kv-cache --fused-kernels --prefetch-policy=dynamic-prototype --metrics=/tmp/m.json
- replay trace (local): python3 replay.py --trace trace-burst.json --concurrency 48 --rate 200 --collect-trace /tmp/trace.json
- extract queue histograms: python3 tools/queue_hist.py /tmp/trace.json > /tmp/queues.csv

Microbench results (representative, median of 5 runs):
- Baseline (no prefetch), fused kernels ON:
  * trace-mix mean latency: 46.2 ms, p95: 118.4 ms, p99: 243.7 ms
- Static prefetch (N=4 tiles), fused ON:
  * trace-mix mean latency: 44.1 ms, p95: 129.3 ms, p99: 305.2 ms (noticeable p99 regression)
- Burst-aware dynamic (this prototype), fused ON:
  * trace-mix mean latency: 43.7 ms, p95: 104.3 ms, p99: 215.8 ms
- Baseline, fused OFF (paged attention path):
  * trace-mix mean: 49.9 ms, p95: 135.6 ms, p99: 299.0 ms
- Dynamic prefetch, fused OFF:
  * trace-mix mean: 48.0 ms, p95: 118.0 ms, p99: 262.4 ms

Observations from traces & kernel-level profiling:
- Kernel queue depth correlates strongly with p95/p99 regressions. Static prefetch increases average kernel duration making queues longer when bursty short requests dominate.
- FlashAttention kernels have better per-token throughput but higher variance when called with variable batch sizes; variance becomes amplified by prefetch that increases occupancy.
- Paged-attention tends to create short-lived page-prefetch artifacts visible as spikes in memory CPI and occasional device-to-host stalls in older runtimes. After updating page prefetch to async scatter (prototype change), spikes reduce but not eliminated.
- Fused ops (attention + rotary + norm) reduce total kernel launches but increase single-kernel runtime; this helps throughput but amplifies tail under queuing.

Heuristic design (burst-aware prototype):
- Burst detector: sliding window (500 ms) counting requests per-second per-device and fraction of requests with seq_len <= 64. If rate > R_thresh and short_fraction > F_thresh, mark device in burst mode for T_burst_ms.
- Prefetch aggressiveness scale: {0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0} mapped to number of tiles/blocks to prefetch. In burst mode, reduce aggressiveness to 0.25 or 0.0 depending on kernel queue_length metric.
- Backpressure signal: if kernel_queue_avg > Q_high, temporarily throttle prefetch and temporarily prefer smaller fused-kernel variants (runtime must expose alternate kernel entry-points).
- Learning kicker: keep short-term EWMA of latency and queue-length; if p95 rises while in reduced prefetch, kick to next lower aggressiveness.

Prototype implementation notes (code changes):
- Prefetch controller implemented as a new thread per device with lock-free ring of request summaries.
- Added small telemetry counters to kernel launcher: launch_latency_ms, kernel_exec_ms, queue_depth_at_launch.
- Introduced policy flags: --prefetch-policy=burst-aware-proto, --prefetch-window-ms, --prefetch-thresholds.

Open experiments and unusual findings:
- Under some burst patterns, reducing prefetch to zero still leaves p99 elevated vs baseline. Hypothesis: prefetch wasn't primary culprit but fused-kernel runtime scheduling and memory controller contention are. Need to instrument DRAM bank utilization and L2 thrash.
- Certain sequence mixes with many mid-length (128–256) show worst impacts — there is a non-linear knee in occupancy where prefetch helps until a concurrency threshold where it hurts. Need a heatmap sweep.
- Replaying production-replay-0310 with simulated network jitter changes the benefit profile — jitter increases burstiness; dynamic detector parameters need tuning.

Immediate mitigations to deploy (low-risk):
1) Expose prefetch aggressiveness knob per-device via runtime config and default to conservative (0.25) for high-concurrency machines.
2) Add a safety cutoff: never prefetch more than X tiles if current kernel_queue_depth > Y.
3) Add metric and alert: sudden rise in kernel_queue_depth or in launch_latency_ms should trigger reduced prefetch mode automatically.

Longer-term work (next sprint):
- Sweep R_thresh, F_thresh, Q_high, and T_burst_ms on a grid using production-replay traces; save configs tagged by traffic shape.
- Integrate a tiny RL-based controller that picks aggressiveness per-device given recent telemetry. Keep it simple (bandit-style).
- Instrument DRAM/L2 metrics and integrate with policy (if device shows high bank contention, lower prefetch).
- Evaluate interaction with autoscaling: prefetch policies may change apparent capacity; ensure autoscaler sees stable SLO signals.

Unresolved questions for the team:
- Do we have alternate kernel entry-points available for smaller fused-kernel variants on all supported GPUs? If not, what is the work to add them? (action: @Marco)
- How to coordinate prefetch policy with Dedicated customers who pin models/variants — need escape hatch and per-customer overrides. (action: product/security)
- Is there value in a user-facing control surface for prefetch aggressiveness vs complexity? Might be confusion for users.

Action items (owners):
- Marco: run heatmap sweep for concurrency 8..256 x seqlen 16..1024 and dump CSVs (due 2024-04-09).
- Priya: add DRAM/L2 counters to profiler and validate under synthetic bank-stress (due 2024-04-16).
- Ethan: prepare canary config with conservative defaults and safety cutoff; coordinate a canary rollout to a non-critical Dedicated cluster (due 2024-04-12).
- Aisha: iterate on the burst detector thresholds with production replay and prepare an RFC for policy rollout (due 2024-04-15).

Notes to self and quick wins:
- Keep default in hosted for now conservative; canary on dedicated where we can control traffic.
- Documented command to dump per-kernel queue histogram is useful for debugging: tools/queue_hist.py --trace /tmp/trace.json --out /tmp/qhist.tsv
- Remember to include seed value for synthetic trace generator in results table for reproducibility.

Appendix: quick reproduction trace snippet (example trace-burst.json event):
{
  "events": [
    {"ts": 0, "seq_len": 32, "tokens": 16, "meta": "user:ux-test"},
    ... (repeated 500x within 10s)
  ]
}

End of prototype notes. This is a working doc — expect updates and new CSVs attached in subsequent revisions.
